name: How much contingency should I add to a restaurant build-out budget?

mainEntity.name: What percentage should I keep aside for surprises in a Los Angeles restaurant project?
mainEntity.text: What percentage should I keep aside for surprises in a Los Angeles restaurant project?

acceptedAnswer.text: Contingency is essential because restaurant build-outs frequently uncover issues that were not visible during initial walkthroughs. Older buildings, reused shells, and concept changes all increase the chance of change orders. The more complex the kitchen and ventilation package, the more likely the project is to encounter structural, mechanical, or utility surprises. A typical contingency range gives the owner flexibility to solve problems without stopping work. For a shell conversion or older storefront, the reserve should trend higher. Owners should treat contingency as part of the real budget, not as optional padding. It protects the opening date and reduces the chance of quality compromises when unexpected work appears.
acceptedAnswer.description: A restaurant build-out budget should usually include a contingency because hidden conditions and permit-driven changes are common. A practical contingency is often around 10% to 20%, with higher reserves for older buildings or complex kitchen conversions.
